canonicalExplanation.summary: `if / else if / else` checks conditions top to bottom and runs **one** branch. Put an explicit `else` for **invalid input** rather than letting it slide into the last band. Java has two switch styles. The **old** `case X:` style **falls through** into the next case unless you `break`. The **modern** arrow style, `case X -> ...`, never falls through, and a **switch expression** returns a value (use `yield` inside blocks). Over an **enum**, a switch expression must cover **every constant** (or have a default), so the compiler catches missing cases. Switching on a **null** String or enum throws NullPointerException, so check first. And always **test the boundaries**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner classifies scores with `if (score > 90) "A" else if (score > 80) "B" ...`, so 90 earns a B and 105 earns an A. Their old-style switch on the day also prints two messages for Friday. A score classifier tests the exact lower and upper boundaries for each band and uses an else branch for invalid input. In this lesson you'll implement and test boundary-complete branching including enum or string cases.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every Java switch case stops automatically and default always makes a decision complete and correct.
misconceptions.correction: Colon-style cases fall through without break, and a default can silently absorb new or invalid values. Arrow cases and exhaustive switch expressions make completeness explicit.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The Friday double message", why did two messages print?

analogy.example: An if/else chain is **a row of sorting bins with exact labels**: "90 to 100", "80 to 89". Anything that fits no bin goes to the **reject tray** (else invalid), not the last bin. An old switch is **a slide** that carries you past your stop unless you grab the rail (break); the arrow switch is **a lift that stops exactly at your floor**.
limitations: Real bins can overflow; your ranges can overlap, so test them.
An exhaustive enum switch is a lift with a button for every floor.

steps.explanation: The classifier tests the exact lower boundary of the A band.
The value just below the boundary lands in the next band.
An else branch handles invalid input instead of guessing a band.

recap.summary: To implement boundary-complete branching, order if/else-if conditions with exact boundaries and an explicit branch for invalid input, use arrow-style switches or switch expressions to avoid fall-through, let exhaustive enum switch expressions catch missing cases, check for null before switching, and test every boundary.
